paragraphs: I shall perhaps be reminded here of a current saying, "that where annual elections end, tyranny begins." It has often been remarked that sayings that become proverbial are generally founded in reason. It is no less true that, once established, they are often applied to cases the reason for them does not reach. I need look no further for proof than the case before us. What is the reason on which this proverbial saying is founded? No one will expose himself to ridicule by pretending that any natural connection exists between the sun or the seasons and the length of time that human virtue can withstand the temptations of power. Happily for mankind, liberty is not confined in this respect to any single point of time. It lies between extremes that leave enough room for all the variations that the different situations and circumstances of civil society may require. The election of public officials might be, if it were found expedient, as in some instances it actually has been, daily, weekly or monthly, as well as annual. And if circumstances may require a departure from the rule on one side, why not on the other also? Turn our attention to the periods established among ourselves for electing the most numerous branches of the State legislatures. We find that they coincide no more in this instance than they do in the elections of other civil officials. In Connecticut and Rhode Island the periods are half-yearly. In the other States, South Carolina excepted, they are annual. In South Carolina they are biennial, as is proposed in the federal government. Here is a difference of four to one between the longest and shortest periods; and yet it would not be easy to show that Connecticut or Rhode Island is better governed, or enjoys a greater share of rational liberty, than South Carolina. Nor could it easily be shown that either the one or the other of these States is distinguished in these respects, and by these causes, from the States whose elections differ from both.

In searching for the grounds of this doctrine, I can discover only one, and that is wholly inapplicable to our case. The important distinction, so well understood in America, between a Constitution established by the people and unalterable by the government, and a law established by the government and alterable by the government, seems to have been little understood and less observed in any other country. Wherever the supreme power of legislation has resided, it has been supposed to hold also a full power to change the form of the government. Even in Great Britain, where the principles of political and civil liberty have been most discussed, and where we hear most of the rights of the Constitution, it is maintained that the authority of Parliament is transcendent and uncontrollable, with regard to the Constitution as much as to the ordinary objects of legislation. Parliament has accordingly, in several instances, actually changed some of the most fundamental articles of the government by legislative acts. In particular, it has on several occasions changed the period of election. On the last occasion it not only introduced septennial in place of triennial elections but, by the same act, continued itself in office for four years beyond the term for which the people had elected it. Attention to these dangerous practices has produced a very natural alarm among the devotees of free government, of which frequent elections are the cornerstone, and has led them to seek some security for liberty against the danger to which it is exposed. Where no Constitution paramount to the government either existed or could be obtained, no constitutional security like that established in the United States could be attempted. Some other security, therefore, had to be sought. And what better security would the case allow than to select and appeal to some simple and familiar portion of time as a standard for measuring the danger of innovations, for fixing the national sentiment, and for uniting patriotic exertions? The simplest and most familiar portion of time applicable to the subject was a year. Hence a laudable zeal, seeking to erect some barrier against the gradual innovations of an unlimited government, has inculcated the doctrine that the advance toward tyranny was to be calculated by the distance of departure from the fixed point of annual elections. But what need can there be to apply this expedient to a government limited, as the federal government will be, by the authority of a paramount Constitution? Or who will pretend that the liberties of the people of America will not be more secure under biennial elections, unalterably fixed by such a Constitution, than those of any other nation would be where elections were annual, or even more frequent, but subject to alteration by the ordinary power of the government?
The second question stated is whether biennial elections are necessary or useful. Several very obvious considerations show that the answer should be yes.

No one can be a competent legislator who does not add to an upright intention and a sound judgment a certain degree of knowledge of the subjects he is to legislate on. Part of this knowledge may be acquired through information within the reach of men in private as well as public stations. Another part can only be acquired, or at least thoroughly acquired, by actual experience in the station that requires its use. In all such cases, therefore, the period of service ought to bear some proportion to the extent of practical knowledge required to perform the service properly. The period of legislative service established in most of the States for the more numerous branch is, as we have seen, one year. The question may then be put in this simple form: does a period of two years bear any greater proportion to the knowledge required for federal legislation than one year does to the knowledge required for State legislation? The very statement of the question in this form suggests the answer that ought to be given.

In a single State, the knowledge required relates to the existing laws, which are uniform throughout the State and with which all the citizens are more or less familiar. It also relates to the general affairs of the State, which lie within a small compass, are not very diversified, and occupy much of the attention and conversation of every class of people. The great theater of the United States presents a very different scene. The laws are so far from uniform that they vary in every State. The public affairs of the Union are spread throughout a very extensive region and are extremely diversified by the local affairs connected with them. They can with difficulty be correctly learned anywhere other than in the central councils, to which a knowledge of them will be brought by the representatives of every part of the empire. Yet the members from each of the States ought to possess some knowledge of the affairs, and even of the laws, of all the States. How can foreign trade be properly regulated by uniform laws without some acquaintance with the commerce, the ports, the usages and the regulations of the different States? How can the trade between the different States be properly regulated without some knowledge of their relative situations in these and other respects? How can taxes be wisely imposed and effectively collected if they are not suited to the different laws and local circumstances relating to these objects in the different States? How can uniform regulations for the militia be properly provided without a similar knowledge of the many internal circumstances that distinguish the States from each other? These are the principal objects of federal legislation, and they suggest most forcibly the extensive information the representatives ought to acquire. The other internal objects will require a proportional degree of information about them.

It is true that all these difficulties will gradually be much diminished. The most laborious task will be the proper inauguration of the government and the original formation of a federal code. Improvements on the first drafts will become both easier and fewer every year. Past transactions of the government will be a ready and accurate source of information for new members. The affairs of the Union will become more and more objects of curiosity and conversation among the citizens at large. And the increased contact among citizens of different States will do much to spread a mutual knowledge of their affairs, and this in turn will contribute to a general assimilation of their manners and laws. But even with all these reductions, the business of federal legislation must continue to exceed the legislative business of a single State, in both novelty and difficulty, by enough to justify the longer period of service assigned to those who are to carry it out.

There is a branch of knowledge that belongs among the acquirements of a federal representative, and that has not been mentioned: foreign affairs. In regulating our own commerce he ought to be acquainted not only with the treaties between the United States and other nations, but also with the commercial policy and laws of other nations. He ought not to be altogether ignorant of the law of nations, for that, so far as it is a proper object of municipal legislation, is committed to the federal government. And although the House of Representatives is not directly to take part in foreign negotiations and arrangements, the several branches of public affairs are necessarily connected. Those particular branches will therefore often deserve attention in the ordinary course of legislation, and will sometimes demand particular legislative sanction and co-operation. Some portion of this knowledge may, no doubt, be acquired in a man's study; but some of it can only be derived from public sources of information; and all of it will be acquired to best effect by practical attention to the subject during the period of actual service in the legislature.

There are other considerations, perhaps of less importance, but not unworthy of notice. The distance many of the representatives will have to travel, and the arrangements that this makes necessary, might be much more serious objections for suitable men to this service if it were limited to a single year than if it were extended to two. No argument can be drawn on this subject from the case of the delegates to the existing Congress. They are elected annually, it is true, but the legislative assemblies consider their re-election almost a matter of course. The election of the representatives by the people would not be governed by the same principle.

A few of the members, as happens in all such assemblies, will have superior talents. By frequent re-election they will become members of long standing, will be thoroughly masters of the public business, and will perhaps not be unwilling to take advantage of this. The greater the proportion of new members, and the less the information of the bulk of the members, the more likely they will be to fall into the snares that may be laid for them. This remark applies no less to the relation that will exist between the House of Representatives and the Senate.

Our frequent elections, even in single States, have advantages, but a drawback is mingled with them where the States are large and hold only one legislative session a year: spurious elections cannot be investigated and annulled in time for the decision to have its proper effect. If a return can be obtained, no matter by what unlawful means, the irregular member, who takes his seat as a matter of course, is sure to hold it long enough to serve his purposes. Hence a very harmful encouragement is given to the use of unlawful means to obtain irregular returns. Were elections for the federal legislature annual, this practice might become a very serious abuse, particularly in the more distant States. Each house is, as it necessarily must be, the judge of the elections, qualifications and returns of its members. Whatever improvements experience may suggest for simplifying and speeding up the process in disputed cases, so great a portion of a year would unavoidably pass before an illegitimate member could be removed from his seat that the prospect of such an event would be little check on unfair and illicit means of obtaining a seat.

All these considerations taken together warrant us in affirming that biennial elections will be as useful to the affairs of the public as we have seen that they will be safe for the liberty of the people.
